stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before migrating, the bar-tailed godwit goes through a striking physical change. The bird, whose nonstop autumn flights from Alaska to New Zealand, the longest recorded for any land bird, have been tracked by satellite since 2007, ______ its body mass in just a few weeks, storing fat while its gizzard and intestines shrink to save weight.
explanation: Remove the 'whose' clause and the subject is left standing alone: 'The bird ______ its body mass.' The verb 'have been tracked' belongs to the 'whose' clause, not to 'The bird,' so the subject still needs a main verb. That rules out every '-ing' form. The subject 'bird' is singular, and the passage is written in the present tense ('goes through'), so the singular present 'doubles' is the only choice that works. The phrase 'storing fat...' after it is a modifier, not a second main verb.

A.why: You took 'have been tracked' as the sentence's main verb, so the '-ing' form seemed to add detail to a sentence that was already complete. 'Have been tracked' sits inside the 'whose' clause, though. Choosing 'doubling' leaves 'The bird' with no verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

B.why: You saw correctly that a finite verb was needed, but you made it agree with the nearby plural nouns 'flights' and 'intestines' instead of the real subject. The subject is 'The bird,' which is singular and needs 'doubles.'

D.why: 'Having doubled' sounds like a finished, polished verb, but it is a participle and cannot be a main verb. The sentence would still have no tensed verb for 'The bird,' so it would be a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sports scientists have long debated whether training in heat helps athletes who compete in cool weather. In a 2021 trial, a team led by physiologist Ines Marlowe tested the question directly. The researchers, who argue in their report that most amateur programs still overlook heat training, put twenty cyclists through ten days of exercise in a 38°C chamber and then ______ each rider's time-trial performance in cool air with that of a control group.
explanation: The subject 'The researchers' has two actions joined by 'and': they 'put' the cyclists through training 'and then ______' the results. The blank is the second half of that compound predicate, so it needs a finite verb that is parallel to 'put.' This rules out 'comparing' and 'to compare.' The trial took place in 2021, and 'put' is past tense here, so the parallel past-tense form is 'compared.' The present-tense 'argue' and 'overlook' belong to the 'who' clause and describe the report, not the experiment.

A.why: You saw correctly that you needed a finite verb, but you matched it to the closest present-tense verbs, 'argue' and 'overlook.' Those verbs are inside the 'who' clause. The verb in the blank is parallel to 'put,' which describes a 2021 experiment, so it has to be past tense: 'compared.'

B.why: 'And then comparing' sounds fluent when you read quickly, but 'and' joins this blank to 'put,' a main verb. An '-ing' form is not parallel to 'put,' and it cannot act as the second main verb of the compound predicate.

C.why: You read the blank as giving the purpose of the training. However, 'and then' marks a second action in a sequence, not a purpose. The infinitive is not parallel to 'put,' so the second half of the compound predicate would have no finite verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Excavators at the hillside site had long dated its lower terrace to the late Bronze Age. The fragments of glazed pottery recovered there last season, along with a single bronze pin whose casting technique matches that of finds from a coastal settlement, ______ that people occupied the terrace several centuries earlier than once assumed.
explanation: The subject of the main clause is "fragments", which is plural, and it has no main verb yet. "Matches" belongs to the "whose" clause and does not count. Since "along with" does not make a subject plural or singular, you cross out everything from "along with" to the comma. That leaves "The fragments ... suggest", which is a finite plural verb.

A.why: You saw that a finite verb was needed, but you matched it to the nearby singular nouns "pin," "technique," or "settlement" rather than to the real subject, "fragments."

B.why: "Suggesting" reads smoothly, but an -ing form can't be a main verb. The subject "fragments" is left with no verb, so the sentence is a fragment. You may have counted "matches" as the main verb, but it belongs to the "whose" clause.

D.why: An infinitive can't serve as the main verb, so "The fragments ... to suggest that..." leaves the sentence without a tensed verb for its subject.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Memory T cells are thought to respond faster to a pathogen they have met before. To test how much faster, a team at a university laboratory in 2019 exposed cultured cells to a modified antigen, tracked how quickly each population divided over five days, and ______ those division rates with the rates of an unmodified control group.
explanation: "A team" has a compound predicate of three actions joined by "and": "exposed," "tracked," and the blank. The last item has to be a finite verb in the same simple past tense, and "in 2019" confirms that tense. "Compared" completes the series.

A.why: "Comparing" sounds natural after a list, but it isn't parallel to "exposed" and "tracked." It leaves the third action without a finite verb.

C.why: The opening "To test" may have made an infinitive seem to fit. But "and to compare" breaks the series of finite past-tense verbs that "a team" governs.

D.why: You correctly chose a finite verb, but you stopped there. "Compares" is present tense, which clashes with "in 2019" and with the parallel past-tense verbs "exposed" and "tracked."

stimulus: Andean weavers often worked on backstrap looms only a forearm's width across. Woven in narrow strips and later stitched into broad panels, the ceremonial cloths that these artisans produced for a single ruling household ______ a thread count so even that the seams are nearly invisible.
explanation: The opening modifier describes "the ceremonial cloths," which is the plural subject. "Produced" is the verb of the "that" clause, so the subject still needs its own main verb. The present-tense plural "display" supplies it and matches "are" later in the sentence.

A.why: You likely took "produced" as the main verb, which made "displaying" look like an add-on modifier. "Produced" belongs to the "that" clause, so "cloths" still has no verb.

B.why: You recognized that a finite verb was needed, but you made it agree with "household," the singular noun right before the blank. The subject is the plural "cloths."

C.why: "Having displayed" is a participle and can't be a main verb, so the sentence remains a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Many mid-century rail lines now sit unused. Converting a city's abandoned freight corridors, which once linked riverfront warehouses to the mills farther inland, into continuous linear parks ______ planners a rare chance to add green space without demolishing any existing buildings.
explanation: The subject is the gerund phrase "Converting ... into continuous linear parks," and a gerund subject is singular. "Linked" is the verb of the "which" clause, so the gerund subject still lacks a main verb. "Gives" is the finite singular verb it needs.

B.why: You saw that a finite verb was needed, but the plurals "corridors," "mills," and "parks" pulled you toward "give." The subject is the act of converting, which is singular.

C.why: Because the sentence opens with an -ing word, you may not have noticed that "Converting ..." is itself the subject. "Giving" leaves that subject with no main verb.

D.why: An infinitive can't be the main verb. With "to give," the long gerund subject never gets a tensed verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The outbreak investigation began in early March. By the time it concluded that summer, the epidemiologists assigned to the county had interviewed more than 4,000 households, many of which reported symptoms the clinics had never recorded, and ______ a cluster of cases traced to a single municipal well.
explanation: "The epidemiologists" has a compound predicate: "had interviewed ... and ___." The "many of which" clause is an interrupter with its own verbs, "reported" and "had recorded," and these don't count. The blank continues the past-perfect predicate, so "identified" works, with "had" carrying over from "had interviewed." "By the time" confirms the past-perfect time frame.

A.why: "To identify" reads as though it states a purpose, but after "and" it has to be parallel to "had interviewed." An infinitive isn't.

B.why: You chose a finite verb, but "identifies" is present tense. It breaks the past-perfect predicate that "By the time it concluded that summer" sets up.

D.why: The finite verbs inside the interrupter may have made the sentence look complete already. "Identifying" isn't parallel to "had interviewed," so the second half of the predicate has no verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Leafy greens supply most of the vitamin K in a typical diet, but nutrition researchers have grown interested in another source. Fermented soybean products such as natto contain menaquinone-7, a form of vitamin K2 that, unlike the K1 found in spinach and kale, ______ in the bloodstream for several days after a meal.
explanation: The main clause already has its verb, "contain." The blank sits inside the "that" clause, though, and that clause needs its own finite verb. The clause's subject is "that," which refers to "a form of vitamin K2," a singular noun. Skip the "unlike ..." interrupter and you get "a form ... that persists."

A.why: You correctly gave the "that" clause a finite verb, but you matched it to "spinach and kale" right before the blank, or to "products." "That" refers to the singular "form."

B.why: Since "contain" already serves as the main verb, you may have assumed the blank could be nonfinite. A "that" clause needs its own tensed verb, though, and an infinitive can't provide one.

C.why: With "persisting," the "that" clause has no finite verb, which leaves it incomplete. You counted "contain" and stopped there.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Engineers searching for better spill-cleanup materials have turned to extremely light solids. Graphene aerogel, a lattice of carbon sheets so sparse that a piece the size of a sugar cube weighs less than three paper clips, ______ up to 900 times its own weight in oil, which makes it a promising option for marine spills.
explanation: "Graphene aerogel" is the singular subject. The appositive between the commas contains its own verb, "weighs," but that verb belongs to the "so sparse that" clause. The subject still needs a main verb, and "absorbs" is the finite singular one. "Its own weight" also confirms that the subject is singular.

A.why: Counting "weighs" or "makes" as the main verb makes "absorbing" look like an extra detail. Both of those verbs sit inside subordinate clauses, so "Graphene aerogel" has no main verb.

C.why: You saw that a finite verb was needed, but the plurals "paper clips" and "sheets" drew you to "absorb." The subject is the singular "Graphene aerogel."

D.why: "Having absorbed" is a participle and can't act as a main verb, so the sentence becomes a fragment. It also changes the meaning to a completed past action.

stimulus: Seismologists cannot drill to Earth's core-mantle boundary, so they study it indirectly. Recorded at monitoring stations spread across three continents, the arrival times of shear waves from a single deep earthquake ______ researchers to estimate how sharply the boundary's composition changes from one region to the next.
explanation: The opening modifier describes "the arrival times," which is the plural subject, and that subject has no verb yet. Once you cross out "of shear waves from a single deep earthquake," you have "the arrival times ... allow." Present tense matches "cannot" and "study."

B.why: You correctly chose a finite verb, but you made it agree with "earthquake," the singular noun right before the blank. The subject is the plural "times."

C.why: Because the sentence opens with the modifier "Recorded ...," it already feels well underway. With "allowing," though, "the arrival times" never gets a main verb.

D.why: "Having allowed" is nonfinite, so the subject still has no tensed verb and the sentence is a fragment.
